triage.name: Sinusitis
triage.reason: Common diagnosis with recognizable symptoms (facial pain, congestion, purulent discharge) and clear distinction between viral and bacterial causes.

demographics: Adults are affected more often than children
More common in people with atopic disease or anatomic nasal obstruction
social_history: Daycare or school exposure to viral infections

chief_complaints.text: My face hurts and feels pressure
My nose is stuffed up and I have thick yellow-green drainage
I have a cough that won't go away, especially at night
I have a headache and feel pressure around my eyes and cheeks

hpi.onset: Gradual, often following a cold that seemed to improve then worsened
hpi.duration: Acute sinusitis lasts up to 4 weeks; symptoms often present for 10 days or more
hpi.progression: Starts as a typical cold with clear runny nose, then after 5–7 days develops thicker purulent discharge, facial pain, and worsening congestion
hpi.location: Face: maxillary (cheeks), frontal (forehead), ethmoid (between eyes), or sphenoid (behind eyes)
hpi.radiation: Pain may radiate to the upper teeth or behind the eyes
hpi.quality: Dull, pressure-like, or throbbing pain; worse when bending forward
hpi.timing: Constant, worse in the morning and with position changes
pertinent_negatives: Tooth pain localized to a single tooth

argues_against: Unilateral severe headache with vision changes

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may not localize facial pain; they present with persistent nasal discharge, cough, irritability, and poor feeding. Fever may be more prominent.
Symptoms may be milder and fever blunted; they may present with confusion or general malaise without prominent facial pain.
Can progress rapidly to severe or invasive fungal sinusitis; symptoms may be atypical and include severe headache, visual changes, or orbital swelling.
Physiologic nasal congestion of pregnancy can mimic or worsen sinusitis; symptoms may be attributed to pregnancy rhinitis.

general.mild: Alert, comfortable, speaking in full sentences; no distress
general.moderate: Mildly uncomfortable, mouth breathing, frequent sniffing or throat clearing
general.severe: Ill-appearing, febrile, splinting face with movement, prefers to sit upright
general.critical: Toxic-appearing with periorbital swelling, proptosis, or altered mental status suggesting orbital or intracranial spread

findings.maneuver: Palpate or percuss over the frontal and maxillary sinuses (forehead and cheeks)
findings.finding: Focal tenderness over the frontal or maxillary sinus

findings.maneuver: Inspect the nasal cavity with a light and anterior rhinoscopy
Inspect the nasal mucosa and turbinates
findings.finding: Erythematous, edematous nasal mucosa with turbinate swelling

findings.maneuver: Examine the posterior pharynx with a tongue blade and light
Transilluminate the maxillary and frontal sinuses in a darkened room
findings.finding: Reduced or absent transillumination on the affected side

findings.maneuver: Inspect the face and periorbital area
Inspect and palpate the orbits, assess extraocular movements
findings.finding: Proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, or decreased visual acuity suggesting orbital cellulitis or cavernous sinus thrombosis
Clear breath sounds without crackles, wheezes, or focal consolidation

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oropharynx with a tongue blade
findings.finding: No tonsillar exudate, uvular deviation, or trismus

findings.maneuver: Assess neck stiffness and perform a brief neurologic screen
findings.finding: No nuchal rigidity, no focal deficits, normal mental status

labs.caveat: Acute bacterial sinusitis is a clinical diagnosis; a normal white count does not exclude it and routine CBC is not required.
Not needed for typical acute sinusitis; marked elevation should raise concern for orbital or intracranial spread.
Low values support a viral cause and can help avoid antibiotics, but it is not part of routine sinusitis workup.

imaging.study: CT of the paranasal sinuses without IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Complications suspected, or when surgery is being planned

findings.text: Mucosal thickening and opacification of one or more paranasal sinuses
Air-fluid level within an affected sinus
Nasal septal deviation or concha bullosa
Orbital or intracranial extension (subperiosteal abscess, epidural or subdural empyema)

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected orbital or intracranial complication, or invasive fungal sinusitis

findings.text: Enhancement and inflammation extending into the orbit or cavernous sinus

imaging.study: Plain radiographs of the paranasal sinuses (Waters, Caldwell, lateral views)

findings.text: Findings are nonspecific and correlate poorly with symptoms

initial.test: CT of the paranasal sinuses without IV contrast
initial.why: Defines extent of disease and anatomy when a complication is suspected or surgery is planned
initial.only_if: orbital or intracranial complication is suspected, or surgery is being considered

initial.test: MRI of the brain and orbits with and without IV contrast
initial.why: Best study for orbital or intracranial spread and for invasive fungal disease
initial.only_if: proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, vision loss, severe headache, or altered mental status

supporting.why: Supports a bacterial process when fever or systemic illness is prominent
supporting.only_if: fever, severe illness, or concern for a complication

supporting.why: Adds objective evidence of bacterial inflammation when the diagnosis is uncertain
supporting.only_if: diagnosis is unclear or a complication is suspected

not_indicated.why: Not needed for uncomplicated acute sinusitis, which is a clinical diagnosis

not_indicated.test: Plain radiographs of the paranasal sinuses (Waters, Caldwell, lateral views)
not_indicated.why: Poor sensitivity and specificity; does not change management

not_indicated.test: MRI of the brain and orbits with and without IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Reserved for suspected orbital or intracranial complications
Routine blood work does not change management of uncomplicated sinusitis
Not required for typical acute sinusitis
Nonspecific and not part of routine workup
No role unless sepsis is suspected

decision_points: Acute bacterial sinusitis is diagnosed clinically: symptoms lasting 10 days or more without improvement, severe symptoms with fever over 102°F and purulent discharge for 3–4 days, or a cold that improves then worsens (double worsening).
Imaging is not needed for uncomplicated acute sinusitis; reserve CT for suspected complications or surgical planning.
Suspect orbital or intracranial extension with periorbital swelling, proptosis, vision changes, severe headache, or altered mental status; obtain urgent MRI or contrast CT.
Consider invasive fungal sinusitis in immunocompromised or poorly controlled diabetic patients with severe symptoms; this is a surgical emergency.

criteria.name: Clinical diagnosis of acute bacterial rhinosinusitis
criteria.summary: Diagnosed when symptoms persist 10 days or more without improvement, or when severe symptoms (fever 102°F or higher, purulent discharge, facial pain) are present for at least 3–4 consecutive days, or when symptoms worsen after initial improvement (double worsening).
items: Symptoms 10 days or more without improvement
Severe symptoms with fever 102°F or higher and purulent discharge for 3–4 days

differential.name: Viral upper respiratory infection (common cold)
differential.why_considered: Most acute sinusitis begins as a viral URI, and the two share congestion, clear-to-mucoid discharge, and mild facial pressure.

history: Symptoms peak in 3–5 days and improve within 7–10 days
Discharge starts clear and thins over time
No double worsening after initial improvement
Low-grade or no fever
exam: Nasal mucosa erythematous but without focal sinus tenderness
No purulent discharge in the middle meatus
Oropharynx may show mild erythema without exudate
labs: Not routinely indicated; viral testing (e.g., influenza, SARS-CoV-2) may identify a specific cause
imaging: Not indicated; sinus imaging is nonspecific and may show mucosal thickening even in uncomplicated viral illness

differential.name: Allergic rhinitis
differential.why_considered: Nasal congestion, clear rhinorrhea, and facial pressure that can mimic sinusitis, especially with seasonal or perennial triggers.

history: Itchy eyes, nose, and throat
Sneezing and watery rhinorrhea
Seasonal or allergen exposure pattern
No purulent discharge or fever
exam: Allergic shiners or transverse nasal crease
labs: Allergen-specific IgE or skin testing may confirm sensitization if diagnosis is unclear
imaging: Not indicated; sinus CT may show incidental mucosal thickening

differential.name: Influenza
differential.why_considered: Fever, myalgias, headache, and respiratory congestion can overlap with acute sinusitis, especially early in the illness.

history: Abrupt onset of high fever, chills, and severe myalgias
Prominent systemic symptoms out of proportion to nasal complaints
Community outbreak or known exposure
exam: Diffuse pharyngeal erythema without focal sinus tenderness
Clear or mucoid nasal discharge early
labs: Positive rapid influenza antigen or molecular test
imaging: Not indicated unless pneumonia is suspected

differential.name: Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis
differential.why_considered: The condition being evaluated; must be distinguished from viral and non-infectious causes to guide antibiotic use.

history: Symptoms 10 days or more without improvement
Severe symptoms with fever 102°F or higher and purulent discharge for 3–4 days
Double worsening after initial improvement
exam: Focal tenderness over maxillary or frontal sinuses
Purulent discharge in the middle meatus
labs: Not required; CBC and CRP may support bacterial process if systemic illness is prominent
imaging: Not indicated for uncomplicated disease; CT reserved for complications or surgical planning

differential.name: Dental infection (odontogenic sinusitis)
differential.why_considered: Maxillary tooth root infection can spread to the maxillary sinus and cause unilateral facial pain and purulent nasal discharge.
differential.trigger: Unilateral maxillary pain with dental tenderness or poor dentition

history: Localized tooth pain or sensitivity to chewing
Recent dental work or known caries
Unilateral symptoms
exam: Dental tenderness or percussion pain over a specific tooth
Possible gingival swelling or sinus tract
labs: Not specific; CBC may show leukocytosis if abscess is present
imaging: Dental radiographs or panoramic X-ray showing periapical abscess
CT of sinuses may show unilateral maxillary sinus opacification with a dental source

differential.name: Orbital cellulitis
differential.why_considered: Sinusitis can spread to the orbit, and orbital cellulitis can present with facial pain, fever, and periorbital swelling that may be mistaken for severe sinusitis.
differential.trigger: Periorbital swelling, proptosis, or vision changes in a patient with sinus symptoms

history: Rapidly progressive periorbital swelling and redness
Pain with eye movement
Blurred or double vision
Recent sinusitis or upper respiratory infection
labs: Blood cultures if systemic signs are present
imaging: Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of orbits and brain showing orbital fat stranding, subperiosteal abscess, or cavernous sinus thrombosis

differential.name: Cavernous sinus thrombosis
differential.why_considered: A rare but life-threatening complication of sinusitis that can present with headache, fever, and cranial nerve deficits.
differential.trigger: Severe headache with cranial nerve palsies (especially CN VI), proptosis, or altered mental status

history: Severe, progressive headache
Diplopia or vision loss
Recent sinusitis or facial infection
exam: Cranial nerve III, IV, or VI palsies
imaging: MRI with MR venography showing filling defect in the cavernous sinus
Contrast-enhanced CT may show enlargement and enhancement of the cavernous sinus

differential.name: Migraine or tension-type headache
differential.why_considered: Headache and facial pain are common in both primary headache disorders and sinusitis, and patients may attribute headache to 'sinus' when no infection is present.

history: Recurrent, stereotyped headaches
Nausea, photophobia, or phonophobia with migraine
No fever, purulent discharge, or anosmia
Headache not worsened by bending forward
exam: Normal nasal exam without purulent discharge
imaging: Not indicated unless red flags for secondary headache are present

severity.mild: Uncomplicated acute sinusitis: congestion, mild facial pressure, low-grade or no fever, able to perform daily activities
severity.moderate: More prominent facial pain, purulent discharge, fever up to 101–102°F, and fatigue limiting some activities
severity.severe: High fever (>102°F), severe facial pain, marked purulent discharge, and systemic symptoms; consider complications and need for imaging
severity.critical: Sinusitis with orbital or intracranial extension (orbital cellulitis, subperiosteal abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, or intracranial empyema), or invasive fungal sinusitis in an immunocompromised patient; requires urgent imaging and specialist care

red_flags.meaning: Orbital cellulitis or abscess; needs urgent imaging and ophthalmology/ENT evaluation
Orbital or cavernous sinus involvement; sight-threatening emergency

red_flags.finding: Severe headache with neck stiffness or altered mental status
red_flags.meaning: Meningitis or intracranial extension; obtain urgent neuroimaging and lumbar puncture if safe

red_flags.finding: Fever >102°F with toxic appearance or hypotension
red_flags.meaning: Sepsis or severe complication; requires urgent workup and resuscitation

red_flags.finding: Facial swelling, numbness, or black eschar in an immunocompromised or diabetic patient
Symptoms lasting >10 days without improvement or double worsening

complications.name: Invasive fungal sinusitis
clues: Black necrotic eschar on nasal mucosa

special_populations.differences: Young children may not localize facial pain; they present with persistent nasal discharge, cough, irritability, and poor feeding. Fever may be more prominent. Complications such as orbital cellulitis can occur and should be suspected with periorbital swelling.
Symptoms may be milder and fever blunted; they may present with confusion or general malaise without prominent facial pain. A high index of suspicion for complications is needed.

Can progress rapidly to severe or invasive fungal sinusitis; symptoms may be atypical and include severe headache, visual changes, or orbital swelling. Early imaging and ENT consultation are critical.

Physiologic nasal congestion of pregnancy can mimic or worsen sinusitis; symptoms may be attributed to pregnancy rhinitis. Treatment should avoid certain antibiotics and decongestants; saline rinses and acetaminophen are preferred.
Poorly controlled diabetes increases risk of invasive fungal sinusitis; suspect with severe symptoms, facial numbness, or black eschar.

key_questions.question: How long have your nasal symptoms been going on?
key_questions.looking_for: 10 days or more without improvement suggests bacterial sinusitis; under 10 days with gradual improvement suggests viral URI

key_questions.question: Did your symptoms start to get better and then get worse again?
key_questions.looking_for: Double worsening after initial improvement supports bacterial superinfection

key_questions.question: What color is your nasal discharge, and has it changed?
key_questions.looking_for: Thick yellow or green purulent discharge; clear discharge that thins over time suggests viral cause

key_questions.question: Where exactly do you feel the pain or pressure in your face?
key_questions.looking_for: Maxillary (cheeks), frontal (forehead), ethmoid (between eyes), or sphenoid (behind eyes) distribution

key_questions.question: Does the pain get worse when you bend forward or lie down?
key_questions.looking_for: Positional worsening of facial pressure supports sinusitis

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever? How high did it get?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever 102°F or higher with purulent discharge for 3–4 days supports bacterial sinusitis

key_questions.question: Do you have a cough, especially at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Postnasal drip causing nocturnal cough is common in sinusitis

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any change in your sense of smell?
Do you have any tooth pain or recent dental problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Localized tooth pain or recent dental work suggests odontogenic sinusitis

key_questions.question: Do you have any vision changes, double vision, or swelling around your eyes?
key_questions.looking_for: Periorbital swelling, proptosis, or vision changes suggest orbital cellulitis or cavernous sinus thrombosis

key_questions.question: Do you have a severe headache, neck stiffness, or confusion?
key_questions.looking_for: Meningismus or altered mental status suggests intracranial extension

key_questions.question: Do you have allergies, asthma, or nasal polyps?
key_questions.looking_for: Atopic disease or anatomic obstruction predisposes to sinusitis

key_questions.question: Have you been using nasal decongestant sprays? For how long?
key_questions.looking_for: Prolonged use can cause rebound congestion mimicking or worsening sinusitis

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or are you exposed to secondhand smoke?
key_questions.looking_for: Smoking or irritant exposure is a risk factor

key_questions.question: Are you immunocompromised or do you have poorly controlled diabetes?
key_questions.looking_for: Risk for invasive fungal sinusitis; suspect with severe symptoms or black eschar

reasoning_points: Symptoms lasting 10 days or more without improvement, severe symptoms with fever 102°F or higher and purulent discharge for 3–4 days, or double worsening after initial improvement support acute bacterial sinusitis
Facial pain or pressure over the maxillary or frontal sinuses, nasal congestion, and purulent nasal discharge are the cardinal features
Postnasal drip, cough (often nocturnal), hyposmia, and fatigue are common associated symptoms
Focal sinus tenderness on palpation and purulent discharge in the nasal cavity support the diagnosis
Viral URI, allergic rhinitis, influenza, and primary headache disorders are important look-alikes to exclude
Red flags such as periorbital swelling, proptosis, vision changes, severe headache, neck stiffness, or altered mental status suggest orbital or intracranial complications and require urgent imaging
Imaging and routine labs are not indicated for uncomplicated acute sinusitis; the diagnosis is clinical

easy: Classic history of a cold that improved then worsened with purulent discharge and facial pain
Symptoms present for more than 10 days without improvement
Focal maxillary or frontal sinus tenderness on exam
medium: Patient with allergic rhinitis and chronic nasal congestion with overlapping symptoms
Mild fever and clear-to-mucoid discharge making viral versus bacterial distinction unclear
Symptoms present for 7–10 days with some improvement, requiring watchful waiting
Unilateral maxillary pain with dental tenderness suggesting odontogenic source
hard: Older adult with blunted fever and confusion but no prominent facial pain
Immunocompromised or poorly controlled diabetic patient with severe headache and facial numbness suggesting invasive fungal sinusitis
Patient with periorbital swelling and proptosis suggesting orbital cellulitis
Young child with persistent nasal discharge, cough, and irritability who cannot localize facial pain
Patient with severe headache and cranial nerve palsy suggesting cavernous sinus thrombosis
